Morning. You folks just moved in, right? I am Greg, I am right across the street.
Hi, I am Gisele. Yes, we are the newcomers. We have been here for about two months.
Two months already. How are you settling in?
Slowly. I am still getting my bearings, honestly. Everything takes me twice as long.
That is normal. I have lived on this block since 1998 and the new grocery store still beats me. So what brought you here?
My husband was transferred. He works for Amazon, and the whole relocation happened in six weeks.
Six weeks. No wonder you are swamped. Listen, if you ever run into me out here, stop and talk. Nobody on this street should keep to themselves.
I would like that. I have not met many people yet, and small talk is exactly what I need to practice.
My husband was transferred, so the whole family moved.

How long have you lived on this street?
Sorry, I have been swamped this week. Let us catch up soon.

When we moved here from Ohio, I think I cried in the car for the first two weeks. I mean, nobody tells you how quiet a new street is at ten in the morning. And the mistake I made, honestly, was that I kept to myself. I stayed inside, I unpacked boxes, I told myself I was too swamped to go out and meet anybody. That only made it worse. What finally helped was the dog, believe it or not. You walk a dog and you run into the same four people every single morning, and after a while the small talk turns into a real conversation. There was a woman two doors down who invited me for coffee in week three, and that was the moment it turned. It took me about six months to really get my bearings, and probably a year before this felt like home. So if you have been here two months and it still feels strange, you are right on schedule.

Hi there, this is Ray Coleman calling from the Fairmont Street Neighborhood Association. This message is going out to everybody on the block, so apologies if you have already heard it twice. We are having our block party on Saturday the fourteenth, starting at four in the afternoon, on the grass at the end of the street. Bring a chair, and if you can, bring one dish to share. We always have plenty of dessert and, you know, almost no salad. The grills and the drinks are covered, so do not worry about that. And if you are a newcomer on the street, please, please come. Honestly, that is the whole reason we do this thing. You will run into half the block in one afternoon. If you can make it, call me back at five five five, zero one four two, or text the same number, and tell me how many of you are coming. Thanks, everybody.

People ask me all the time how long it takes to feel at home in a new country, and I always give the same annoying answer. Longer than you want, and less time than you think. The first three months are the worst, and here is why. Everything that used to be automatic suddenly costs you energy. Buying shampoo is a project. A phone call is a project. You are swamped by things that are not even difficult, they are just unfamiliar. And on top of that you have no small talk yet, because small talk runs on shared references, and you do not have them. What changes it, in my opinion, is not the language. It is repetition. One day you run into somebody you know at the store, and you have a normal, boring conversation about the weather, and you walk out and realize you have started to settle in without noticing.
